catalog_quote: All 7 vowels can bear a tone – high (marked as ʹ above the vowel) or low (unmarked) and be lengthened (disregarding the tone type), for example: kɔgɔ́pa ‘to fear’ vs. mogɔɔŋgɔ ‘back [body part]’. new_statements.rule_in_words: Isanzu is described as a two-tone (H/L) language with contrastive vowel length; the only first-hand description says nothing whatever about word stress or accent, and the authors state their data were insufficient to characterise even the tone system. No stress position can be assigned.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the authors explicitly decline to generalise about tone.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (elicited Swadesh-list words and short sentences); tone marked on vowels of citation forms; no phrase-level prosody discussed.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted source describes Isanzu proper (isan1243; speakers' name Kiihanzu, Maho F31B 'Isanzu' dialect of Nilamba F31) from one 38-year-old male consultant recorded at Haydom (Manyara region). The Johnson 1923-26 material examined for context is Nilamba/Kiniramba (nila1242), which Johnson himself says is 'not so much akin' to Isanzu; nothing from it is attributed to Isanzu.

tone_statements.citation: Harvey, Andrew & Daisuke Shinagawa. 2020. Tone in Ihanzu. Talk given at the Rift Valley Webinar Series, 11 March 2020. Video recording (mp4, 98.6 MB) deposited on Zenodo (Rift Valley Network community; record title 'Tone in Uhanzu'). DOI 10.5281/zenodo.3707591. CC BY 4.0.
tone_statements.quote: Ihanzu possesses two phonemic tone contrasts: low (zero) and high. This talk, incorporating audio recordings from recent fieldwork, explores and demonstrates the layers of rules which dictate the instantiation of tone in this language.
tone_statements.summary: Privative H vs L(=zero) lexical tone contrast with a set of tone realisation rules (rule details unseen, in the video).

sources.note: Nothing about stress or accent (a full-text search for stress/accent|accent|penult = 0 hits). Says Isanzu has '2 level tones (H, L)' (abstract, p. 4); p. 8: all 7 vowels bear H or L tone and can be lengthened, 'Our data was not sufficient to make any generalisations about nature and functions of tone'; p. 11: lengthening and tones not marked in the practical orthography. sources.note: Comparative phonology/lexicostatistics of Sukuma-Nyamwezi-Sumbwa with other zone-F lects (incl. 'KiniHaanzu = Isanzu') as comparison wordlist data; Glottolog types it a wordlist or less for Isanzu. a full-text search for stress/accent the (poor) scanned text for stress|accent|penult finds only a remark that penultimate syllables tend to lengthen their vowels in JinaKiiya (Sukuma) verbs; no Isanzu stress or tone statement found. scanned caveat: the language name is mangled (one hit 'KlnrHaanzu', about reflexes of PB *c).

sources.note: Talk abstract only: distal-1 demonstratives are formed like medial ones but bear a high tone on root o (ayo vs ayóó), a grammatical tone contrast; no inventory or analysis; video not transcribed.

tone.quote: Medial demonstrative pronouns are used to refer to something that is not far away from both speaker and hearer. They are formed by noun class prefix reduplication attached to the root o (ɨmaje ayo ‘these eggs’). Distal demonstrative pronouns of subtype 1 are used to refer to something that is far away from both speaker and hearer. They are formed in the same way as medial but are pronounced with the hight tone on the root o (ɨmaje ayóó ‘those eggs’).
